background.fact: Apple developed the AIFF family; AIFF-C extended it to compressed sound in August 1991.
AIFF-C stores sampled audio in an AIFF-related wrapper.
An AIFC file can contain uncompressed samples, despite the C in its name.
Python’s AIFF-C interface documents NONE, ULAW, ALAW, and G722 compression identifiers.
Channel count, sample width, and sampling frequency describe the stored sound.
AIFF-C can include markers identifying positions within the recording.

windows.note: Reads AIFF-C through its AIFF demuxer; decoding depends on the stored encoding.
Uses FFmpeg libraries for playback.
Opens AIFC, including common compressed AIFF variants and files with up to 32 channels.

mac.note: Reads AIFF-C through its AIFF demuxer; decoding depends on the stored encoding.
Uses FFmpeg libraries for playback.
Opens AIFC, including common compressed AIFF variants and files with up to 32 channels.

linux.note: Reads AIFF-C through its AIFF demuxer; decoding depends on the stored encoding.

problems.fact: A recognized AIFC wrapper can still contain a codec that the reader does not implement.
Audition opens common compressed AIFF variants, but does not promise every variant.
In Audition, AIFF author information appears under Dublin Core: Creator in the XMP metadata view.

background.fact: MPV is used for MPEG video files; Adobe groups this suffix with MPEG-1 imports.
A raw MPEG video stream has no program-stream wrapper.
FFmpeg distinguishes raw video sequences from MPEG packets that contain audio.
Adobe Media Encoder lists MPV among its recognized MPEG input extensions.
The extension alone should not be used to decide whether MPEG-1 or MPEG-2 decoding is needed.

windows.note: Its raw MPEG demuxer recognizes video sequences from their contents.
Plays through the FFmpeg libraries when MPEG decoding is included.
Lists .mpv in its MPEG-1 import extensions.

mac.note: Its raw MPEG demuxer recognizes video sequences from their contents.
Plays through the FFmpeg libraries when MPEG decoding is included.
Lists .mpv in its MPEG-1 import extensions.

linux.note: Its raw MPEG demuxer recognizes video sequences from their contents.
Plays through the FFmpeg libraries when MPEG decoding is included.

problems.fact: A raw video elementary stream has no companion soundtrack inside its video data.
Premiere Elements lists MPV among unsupported file extensions; After Effects has a different import list.
Adobe warns that changing an MPEG filename extension does not guarantee import compatibility.

background.fact: 3G2 belongs to the multimedia file-format family specified by 3GPP2.
It uses the ISO media file-format family as its foundation.
The wrapper can contain sound, moving pictures, and timed text.
RFC 4393 registered its media types in March 2006.
The preferred filename ending is .3g2; .3gpp2 is also identified.
The audio/3gpp2 label is restricted to files without visual material.
The video/3gpp2 label is valid for 3G2 content even when it contains only audio.

windows.note: Registers .3g2 with its QuickTime and ISO base media demuxer.
Uses the FFmpeg demuxers and decoders.
Recognizes .3g2 as an import extension.

mac.note: Registers .3g2 with its QuickTime and ISO base media demuxer.
Uses the FFmpeg demuxers and decoders.
Recognizes .3g2 as an import extension.

linux.note: Registers .3g2 with its QuickTime and ISO base media demuxer.
Uses the FFmpeg demuxers and decoders.

problems.fact: A video/3gpp2 file may be audio-only, so a missing picture is not always a playback failure.
Timed text counts as visual content and should not be labeled audio/3gpp2.
Text-style transfer that changes line endings or strips high bits can corrupt this binary format.

background.fact: Microsoft’s Enhanced Metafile stores graphics as recorded drawing operations.
An EMF contains a header, drawing records, and an end record.
Records describe graphics objects, property changes, and drawing orders.
Its device-independent design keeps drawing proportions across output devices.
EMF’s first extension added a pixel-format record and OpenGL command support.
RFC 7903 identifies image/emf and the older image/x-emf media type.

windows.note: Lists Enhanced Windows Metafile among its import formats.
Its format matrix lists EMF input and output support.

mac.note: Lists Enhanced Windows Metafile among its import formats.
Its format matrix lists EMF input and output support.

linux.note: Lists Enhanced Windows Metafile among its import formats.
Its format matrix lists EMF input and output support.

problems.fact: A damaged record length can prevent a reader from locating the next drawing record.
Older EMF readers may not implement records introduced by the format’s extensions.
Import support does not establish complete fidelity: Inkscape warns that some imported formats lose unsupported features.

background.fact: The .rmvb suffix identifies variable-bitrate RealMedia video in the RealNetworks family.
RealVideo supports encoding toward an average bitrate or a constant visual quality.
RealVideo 9 and 10 differ in coding efficiency, according to the Library of Congress description.
RealMedia can hold descriptive information such as title, author, and copyright.
The Library of Congress lists application/vnd.rn-realmedia for these RealMedia files.
RealPlayer HD explicitly includes playback support for existing RMVB videos.

windows.note: Includes a RealMedia demuxer and codec-specific handling.
Plays supported RealMedia streams through FFmpeg libraries.
The vendor lists RMVB playback and Windows system requirements.

mac.note: Includes a RealMedia demuxer and codec-specific handling.
Plays supported RealMedia streams through FFmpeg libraries.

linux.note: Includes a RealMedia demuxer and codec-specific handling.
Plays supported RealMedia streams through FFmpeg libraries.

problems.fact: A player needs both the RealMedia reader and a decoder for the audio or video it finds.
FFmpeg rejects invalid RealMedia headers rather than treating every .rmvb name as readable media.
Some RealMedia streaming workflows use a separate .ram reference file; it is not the video payload.

background.fact: GSM 06.10 is a lossy speech codec specified by ETSI.
The RPE-LTP algorithm targets telephone speech at 13 kbit/s.
The libgsm implementation packs each 160-sample input block into a 264-bit frame.
The toast utility writes compressed speech with the .gsm ending.
FFmpeg’s raw GSM reader uses mono audio and an 8,000 Hz default sample rate.
Microsoft’s WAV GSM packing differs from the raw framing used by libgsm.

windows.note: Reads raw .gsm frames and exposes them as mono speech.
Can play GSM through FFmpeg's reader and decoder.

mac.note: Reads raw .gsm frames and exposes them as mono speech.
Can play GSM through FFmpeg's reader and decoder.

linux.note: Reads raw .gsm frames and exposes them as mono speech.
Can play GSM through FFmpeg's reader and decoder.
The libgsm command-line utilities encode and decode raw GSM speech.

problems.fact: Repeated GSM compression removes more information and can create audible chirping.
Raw .gsm and WAV format 49 use incompatible framing, so they are not interchangeable byte layouts.
A truncated final block is invalid to FFmpeg’s raw GSM reader, which expects complete 33-byte blocks.

background.fact: JPS stores a stereoscopic picture using JPEG compression.
A typical JPS arranges the two eye views side by side for crossed-eye viewing.
The VRex proposal described stereo-layout information in a JPEG APP3 marker.
StereoPhoto Maker treats the picture’s file type separately from its stereo layout.
StereoPhoto Maker supports layouts including side-by-side, above/below, and interlaced views.
JPS can carry an embedded preview thumbnail as a JPEG-format image.

windows.note: Reads JPS stereo markers and interprets .jps as a crossed-eye image pair.
Directly opens JPS and lets you choose the stereo arrangement.
Its release history documents JPS descriptor support for automatic layout recognition.

mac.note: Reads JPS stereo markers and interprets .jps as a crossed-eye image pair.
The vendor provides a Wine-based Mac package; its JPS reader is documented in the shared help.

linux.note: Reads JPS stereo markers and interprets .jps as a crossed-eye image pair.

mobile.note: Reads JPS stereo markers and interprets .jps as a crossed-eye image pair.

problems.fact: Selecting the wrong stereo arrangement can display the eye views incorrectly.
A JPS extension does not guarantee that every reader will infer its layout; StereoPhoto Maker asks the user to specify it.
Re-saving a JPS through JPEG output applies the selected compression quality again; keep the source when editing.

background.fact: DOT is Microsoft’s legacy Word template extension.
Microsoft labels it the Word 97–2003 Template format.
A template provides a starting point for new documents rather than one finished document.
The newer DOTX template uses the XML-based Word format.
DOTM is the newer macro-enabled template choice, distinct from DOTX.
LibreOffice Writer includes .dot in its supported legacy Word imports.

windows.note: Reads legacy Microsoft Word .dot templates.
Its file-management documentation lists .dot import.
Supports the legacy Word 97–2003 template format.

mac.note: Reads legacy Microsoft Word .dot templates.
Its file-management documentation lists .dot import.
Supports the legacy Word 97–2003 template format.

web.note: Displays legacy DOT; editing saves a new modern-format copy rather than overwriting DOT.

mobile.note: Microsoft’s iPhone compatibility table lists binary .dot templates as readable and editable.

problems.fact: To change the template itself, open it through Word’s File > Open command and save the template after editing.
Modern Word templates that need macros use DOTM; DOTX is the macro-free choice.
Word for the web cannot save in the old DOT format; editing creates a DOTX or DOCX copy.
